articles.text: Since 1968, Beach Elementary School has presented a musical revue. With over 85% of families participating, the Beach Revue is truly a community effort. The Beach community celebrates 55 years of the Revue with this year’s theme of “Runaway Magic.” The audience can expect an exuberant and fun-filled show, featuring many memorable magical worlds presented by Beach students of all ages in full color. Presentations this weekend mark the culmination of a marathon community endeavor of theater, song, dance and fun. “There are dozens and dozens of parents who spend a ton of time on the Beach Revue every year,” said parent volunteer Marty McCall “I’ve been working on it since July. We put our heart and soul into it.” Shows at the Alan Harvey Theater at Piedmont High begin at 6:30 p.m. on Friday, March 7 and Saturday, March 8. The final performance is at 2:00 p.m. on Sunday, March 9. Tickets may be purchased at Piedmont.city/ beachrevue. Tickets are $25 for adults and $15 for students and children. All proceeds benefit Beach Elementary School. Beach School students work on choreography in the school auditorium on January 12 for the Beach Revue.

articles.text: Piedmont’s City Council received an update on progress of construction on the Community Pool at their meeting on Monday, March 3. The report stated June 2, 2025 as the completion date for construction, roughly one year later than originally planned. The date does not account for possible further delays due to weather and also does not include a period of four weeks for testing all systems. Key project updates included insulation and drywall on the interiors, solar panel installation, and permanent power turned on by PG&E. Following rains in January and February this year, construction was stalled as workers waited for the site to dry enough to excavate the smaller non-competitive pool. Crews began soil removal on Friday, February 28, and excavation for the activity pool is expected to be completed by the end of March. Once both pools are filled with water, the project will enter a phase known as “commissioning,” when the mechanical, electrical, and building management systems that control the facility are tested to ensure they are working properly. This commissioning process is particularly important for Piedmont’s project, as it is one of the first all-electric municipal pools in California. The first all-electric municipal pool, located in the City of Mountain View, started construction in spring 2022 and had a commissioning process that reportedly took months to complete. An expected opening date for Piedmont’s community pool will not be announced until the commissioning process is underway. But the reality is that this 11’-0” “Flagpole” slice of land is first and foremost a “pedestrian way” or a “path of travel”. It is the means of egress to Howard Avenue as it provides the only fire exiting system from the proposed condominiums that are over 110’ up the hill on the small Flag portion of the property. I would like Piedmont Post readers to imagine a Flag Lot that has retaining walls on each boundary lot line separating it from a contiguous property. pages.text: Wednesday, March 5, 2025 3 LETTERS - MAIN The dangers of flag lot at 210 Howard By Bernie Stein Editor: When I read last week that the Piedmont Walkers went by “to see the disputed 210 address site...with a narrow driveway up the hill”, I was reminded that most people see the narrow “Flagpole” portion of the lot going up the hill as only a driveway. But the reality is that this 11’-0” “Flagpole” slice of land is first and foremost a “pedestrian way” or a “path of travel”. It is the means of egress to Howard Avenue as it provides the only fire exiting system from the proposed condominiums that are over 110’ up the hill on the small Flag portion of the property. I would like Piedmont Post readers to imagine a Flag Lot that has retaining walls on each boundary lot line separating it from a contiguous property. Next, imagine 6-foot high fences without any exit gates or doors in them, built on top of (or next to) these boundary retaining walls. Then, please consider that the proposed paved “Flagpole” slopes up 20% from Howard Avenue and has cross slopes of close to 21% without any Building Code required ramps or stairs in it. Lastly, I would like folks to imagine being trapped on the “Flagpole” portion of the lot when there is a fire on the hill where the condominiums are located. Think about the confusion and panic when people are moving slowly down the steep slope that has no stairs or ramps at the same time the owners of the cars in the 4 car garage are trying to get their vehicles safely down to Howard. At the same time, think about the first responders rushing up this pedestrian way/driveway with hoses to attach to new hydrants on the hill. This project is a recipe for disaster. But thank goodness there is the California Building Code and Piedmont Public Works Standard Details to provide building and site health and safety requirements as well as standards for construction which places pedestrian safety before vehicular use on a property. The reality is that after the project’s retaining walls are provided on the Flagpole portion of the 210 Howard lot, I believe the actual paved walking/driving surface between the walls will be between 8’ and 9’ wide, not be the 10’ wide space shown in the applicant’s drawings. It appears that the owner/developer assumed that the neighbors would grant permission to access their properties and build project construction items, such as subsurface geotextile fabric and perforated drain tile (which are shown in the engineer’s structural details) on their properties. By not accounting for these items, only then can the applicant show the pedestrian/vehicular passageway as a 10’ wide space. Piedmont’s own Division 17.54, which the City wrote for SB 9 Lot Splits and Two Unit Housing Developments, requires a minimum 36” wide “path of travel” to any new SB 9 unit from a street. Without getting into the weeds where I identify specific California Building Code divisions and sections, the Building Code considers any walking surface, or “path of travel” with a slope greater than 5%, as a ramp. The developer/owner is showing almost half of the “path of travel”/driveway as having a running slope of 20%. Putting ADA standards aside, the California Building Code requires the construction of either stairs or ramps in the portions of the project’s “path of travel”/driveway where the slope exceeds 5% to allow for a safe, code compliant means of egress to Howard Avenue. Depending on the slope of the ramp, or the number of risers in the stair system, handrails might be required on one or two sides of these egress system components. If a ramp system were to be constructed, in all probability, intermediate landings will be required. Ramps and stairs also may have 4” or 6” high curbs on their edges. So, there is a good chance that the proposed 20% sloping portion of this passageway will have physical elements that prevent a vehicle from going down the “Flagpole” portion. Many Bay Area cities require that the “Flagpole” portion of a Flag Lot have a minimum width of 16’ to 20’ to allow for safe pedestrian and vehicular access at the same time, thus recognizing properties that have sloping terrains. 210 Howard Avenue’s 11’ wide “Flagpole” presents a specific, adverse impact upon its residents health and safety, as well as that of the neighborhood. Short of purchasing land from adjoining neighbors to widen the “Flagpole”, I don’t see a way to mitigate or avoid this specific safety impact. And I don’t think a neighbor will sell a piece of their developed property for this purpose. articles.text: Piedmont City Staff unveiled a new online public record request system at the March 3 City Council meeting, allowing community members to submit, track progress, and review responses to their public records requests entirely online. Use of the online system, called NextRequest, was demonstrated at the meeting by City Clerk Anna Brown. NextRequest is available at piedmont.ca.gov/PRA. The system also allows anyone to view requests and responsive documents submitted by other community members, creating a “one stop shop” for all activities related to public record requests. A demonstration of the system is available on Youtube at https:// www.youtube.com/watch?v=LjKNBPnB-NQ. The platform collects all actions and information related to an individual records request, including clarifying questions and responsive documents, on a single page that can be viewed anytime, by anyone. State law mandates that cities provide records related to operations, activities, and decision-making processes to the public by request within certain timeframes. This can include documents, emails, maps, audio and video recordings, and photographs. Many public records, such as meeting agendas and videos, audited financial statements, and campaign finance reports are already available online. For records not readily available online, the City previously managed requests primarily through email, which could quickly become unwieldy, especially for complex requests. The new system aims to improve the speed, convenience and transparency of public record requests in Piedmont. The launch of NextRequest is part of the City’s ongoing effort to modernize operations, including making more services available online. This is one of several technology upgrade projects planned for 2025, which also include online business licensing and a new City website. articles.text: Rewarding tasks motivate us; however, in school students are faced everyday with tasks that are not intrinsically rewarding but still need to be done. To do this requires effort – and effort requires motivation. Research studies show that effort requires the activation of executive functions (e.g. initiating, planning, and sustaining attention). ADHD is associated with dysfunction in the areas of the brain that control executive functions, which results in those with ADHD having a stronger gravitational pull towards a type of cognitive resting state that increases daydreaming or for the mind to be engaged in another task. As a result, for a student to escape from this resting state requires more effort than is typical to shift attention to the task at hand. In other words, a student with ADHD requires more motivation to accomplish tasks that are not intrinsically rewarding such as homework. Many ADHD-related behaviors such as procrastination, inattention, poor planning, and unfinished work are the result of this need for increased motiKids with ADHD can struggle with homework. vation being unfulfilled. By recognizing this brain function, the student can be supported by being given stronger incentives, immediate rewards, and frequent reinforcement to learn optimally. In addition, children with ADHD who are struggling with their ability to accomplish tasks that lack inherent rewards will benefit from prompts and cues redirecting their attention, being asked to repeat back multistep instructions before starting a task, and having a safe environment to ask for directions to be repeated. They also benefit from interventions such as hands-on and arts-integrated lessons that naturally boost the reward (dopamine) systems in the brain. Excitingly, due to the developmental elasticity of the brain, these types of appropriate support and strategies taught by understanding teachers can actually serve to rewire the brain to develop more efficient networks and lead to positive outcomes for those with ADHD. Nancy Rowland is Head of School at Orinda Academy, an intentionally small independent high school that supports students who think and learn differently. She can be reached at nancy@orindaacademy.org.
articles.title: Adolescent motivation complicated by ADHD

articles.text: The Califor nia Mobile Museum of Tolerance (MMOT) will be coming to Piedmont schools March 3-7. The Mobile Museum of Tolerance, an initiative of the Simon Wiesenthal Center, is a stateof-the-art traveling museum dedicated to promoting human rights, diversity, and respect. Through interactive and engaging workshops, MMOT challenges participants to confront issues such as intolerance, hate, and discrimination, empowering them to be upstanders in their communities. This is an opportunity for students to experience the impactful work the MMOT is doing to educate and inspire students throughout California. Piedmont middle and high school students will have scheduled visits on the bus while school is in session and we are excited to share that Monday-Wednesday evenings at 6pm and 7pm, greater community members will have the opportunity to experience the powerful workshops as well. Bringing the MMOT to schools is a crucial step in fostering dialogue and understanding among young people. Community presence underscores the importance of this mission and demonstrates a shared commitment to educating future generations on the values of inclusivity and respect. Register at https://tinyurl.com/ MMOTPiedmont. Each session is one hour and can accommodate 30 people. Sessions are free. The Power of Ordinary People Grades 8-12 and older Learning Objectives: This workshop helps participants understand the powerful roles individuals can play in either supporting or opposing hate and violence. This workshop equips participants to recognize their own capacity to be agents of change. Fact or Fiction? (Digital Media Literacy Workshop) Grades 9-12 and older Learning Objectives: This workshop equips participants with skills to critically evaluate digital content for authenticity. This workshop empowers students to become discerning consumers of digital media. More details about the MMOT modules can be found on the mobile museum’s website at www.mmot.com.

articles.text: The Piedmont Middle School (PMS) Parents Club is now selling tickets for a PMS fundraiser on Thursday, March 27, “Kickin’ It Old Skool.” This is the school’s biggest fundraiser and will take place at Piedmont Community Hall from 7:00-10:00 p.m. Party-goers will eat, drink, and dance the night away to favorite music from the 80’s and 90’s. The Kickin’ it Old Skool event, formerly known as “March Mingle,” will feature a live auction with special items including a Lake Tahoe vacation rental, a sunset cruise catered by Trader Vic’s, and sporting event tickets. Old school sneakers like Vans and Keds are recommended. There will also be a raffle and surprises that can be described as “totally radical.” Don’t miss the rare opportunity to relive memories of junior high school days and the culture unique to the era. The event will be co-chaired by Melissa Emanuelson and Heidianne Pillsbury. As a bonus, the good vibes promise to keep rolling after the main event with several Parent Parties, including a Pub Quiz night and Intro to Poker. The PMS Parents Club hopes the parents parties will help raise funds to support school programs. “Heidianne and I are thrilled to be leading an event so crucial to the day-to-day success of our middle school kids and the exceptional teachers and administrators who guide them,” Emanuelson said. “I’m especially hoping to see many of my fellow 5th grade parents on March 27, knowing the positive impact we can make on our kids’ education for the next three years.” “There’s so much development and change happening in the middle school,” added Pillsbury. “I’m so thankful for the amazing counselors and mental health resources available to our kids, but they’re not guaranteed. This event is crucial to raising the funds to keep them going.” Funds will support: • Counselor/Mental Health resources and events • Lunch Clubs • After School Tutoring • DEI Programming (Diversity Day, movies in celebration of culture each month) • Library Subscriptions • Emergency Preparedness Supplies • 6th Grade Welcome Programs (including Scots Camp) The PMS Fundraiser team is seeking out a few more Parent Sponsors. articles.text: Piedmont High opens season with strong performance Piedmont High School swim team made a splash in their season opener, securing victories against both Hayward and Bishop O’Dowd in a tri-meet. New head coach Adrien Downey was pleased with the team’s performance, not just in terms of results but also in their camaraderie and focus. “The highlights for me were all about chemistry,” Downey said. “The team did a good job switching it on during warm-ups and psyching each other up. The meet flew by, but our relays and individual racers stayed composed and moved as a team rather than as scattered individuals.” Among the standout performances, Sydney Olson showcased remarkable resilience by competing in back-to-back sprints in the 50 freestyle and 100 butterfly with little rest. “The toughness she showed in keeping up with the fast meet flow stands in for our entire team effort in my eyes,” Downey noted. Tai March-Cunningham and Inaya Majid also stepped up by tackling events outside their comfort zones, demonstrating leadership and team-first attitudes. On the boys’ side, Owen Blanford held on for a thrilling victory in the 100 freestyle, with Nik Costello making a late charge from the outside to secure second place. The junior varsity boys, though a small group, made a big impact with their energy and determination, particularly in relay events. articles.text: Staff Photos Ravi Silverberg takes a 3-pointer with Piedmont’s student section behind him. He led the team with 33 points against St. Patrick. Piedmont’s No. 1 seeded boys’ basketball team almost battled back for the Division 4 North Coast Section title against No. 11 St. Patrick but fell short of a comeback in a 75-70 loss on Saturday, March 1 at San Leandro High School’s new gym. The Highlanders whittled away a 21 point deficit late in the third quarter to three points but couldn’t take the lead. “I’ve told the guys all year that heart can only get you so far. You can’t spot teams leads, and that’s what we’ve done all year. We don’t come ready and have to battle back. That happened today. But I’m proud of how they battled and how hard they played,” coach Ben Spencer said. Fighting from behind has been a common trend for Piedmont this season. The Highlanders mounted several comebacks this year, including in an overtime win against University on January 11 and a one-point 61-60 victory over San Leandro on January 31. This time, the gap was too far to overtake. “I think it has happened because we’re not locked in enough. If we can build an early lead for ourselves, we can withstand runs from other teams. It’s about how we start the game. We have to get defensive stops and stack them, I think that’s a big factor,” said senior leader Ravi Silverberg. It was one of Silverberg’s highest scoring performances of his high school career with 33 points. “When I saw there were seven minutes left, I thought, ‘I’m going to give it all I’ve got.’ Playing with four fouls, I knew I had to play smarter but still play aggressively without fouling,” Silverberg said. Second-chance points were a big part of the Bruins’ win after nabbing offensive rebounds. “They probably had around 20 second-chance points,” observed Spencer. “If we cleaned up half of those boards, we may have taken the game. Rebounding can be a toughness thing; we didn’t come out tough in that first half,”. But Piedmont’s season isn’t over. PHS cut the Bruins’ lead to 17-14 after Casey hit a 3-pointer, but SPSV scored six and allowed two to end the first with a 23-16 advantage. In the second quarter, Casey opened with a pair of baskets to make it 25-20, but St. Patrick then scored five straight to build a 30-20 advantage with 5:50 on the clock. Piedmont chipped away to a five-point deficit at 34-29 when Silverberg converted a pair of free throws but SP scored six of the next seven points to lead 41-30 with 40 seconds left. Casey hit a field goal to make it 41-32 at the half. But PHS went cold in the third. After Silverberg hit a three and Fang-Ring turned a steal into a layup to make it 51-41, the Bruins established its 21-point lead by scoring 12 of the next 13 points including 10 straight. Piedmont began marching down SPSV in the fourth, pulling it to 66-56 with 4:18 left after Silverberg hit a 3-pointer and layup on successive possessions. However, Casey fouled out with 3:52 left, giving SP a 68-56 advantage which extended to 70-57. From there, Piedmont scored nine straight points with threes by Silverberg and Beach Lorin to make it 70-65 with 1:53 left. After a St. Patrick free throw, Lorin converted a layup to make it 71-68 with one minute left— but that was the closest it got. St. Patrick made a layup of its own with 44.8 left, then added a free throw to extend to 74-68. Lorin and Silverberg hit one of two three throws from there, but that was it for Piedmont. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team, the No.1 seed, saw its dream of a third North Coast Section title in four years fell short, losing 2-0 to No. 2 Roseland University Prep in the Div. 4 finals on Saturday, March 1 on a cold and drizzly night at Witter Field. The Knights scored both of their goals in the first half by way of successive corners. In a physical game, Piedmont played 30 minutes with a man-advantage, but still couldn’t find the net. “We just didn’t have enough quality with two set pieces we gave away. We had the numerical advantage and superiority in terms of players positions; we had front four and five at some points. We got frantic and I think the moment got to the boys. But it’s a great learning experience for them and I think the life lessons out of this are huge,” coach Ben Russell said, who is finishing up his first season as head coach. The Highlanders couldn’t replicate its smooth transition play and counter-attacking ability it showed in the early rounds of the playoffs. Bini agreed with Russell that the championship moment psyched some players out. “It got rowdy out there and we got a little rattled; we let the emotions get away from us. It’s tough to see us fall apart like that, but I know it’s a learning moment,” said Bini, a senior and team captain. Roseland’s opening goal came when Piedmont allowed a rolling pass from a corner to the top of the box, leading to a wicked curling shot by Angel Guzman, who scored both of RUP’s goals. Russell would’ve liked to see his team attack the ball to start a counter with the Knights committing a lot of players in the box. “We had the mindset that we’re defending the set piece rather than taking it as a counter-attack pass. Fair play to them, they executed really well. But our mindset needs to be its our counterattack rather than we’re defending their corner. If we can attack the ball instead of following their man, that’s the mindset I want. Obviously it takes time to develop that,” Russell said. Piedmont drew 10 corner kicks on the night, but couldn’t generate a goal on set pieces, This season, PHS has proven to be very productive from set pieces and corners, but it wasn’t the same on Saturday. Piedmont advances to NorCal tourney But Piedmont’s season isn’t over. With the Finals appearance, they clinched a berth in the Division 5 CIF State NorCal tournament as the No. 5 seed. They traveled to No. 4 Orland outside of Chico on Tuesday, March 4, results were not complete by Post time. articles.text: Team now advances to NorCal playoffs Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team, the No.5 seed, solidified itself as a top-five North Coast Section team. On Wednesday, February 26, they beat No. 6 seed Salesian 70-48 in the Open Division’s Fifth-Place Final at Binks Rawlings Gym. The Highlanders never trailed, dominating the boards with 47 total rebounds. Piedmont held a narrow five-point 29-24 lead early in the third quarter and expanded it to 22 by the end of the game. Sophomore Taylor White led the way with 15 rebounds. “We really wanted to focus on rebounds this game and keep Salesian off the boards. In the third quarter, we got things started and it really made a difference. Our energy and ball-movement was really key, we made a lot of cross-court passes to Savannah [Dennig]. We were finding people down low on the block and breaking their press,” White said. It was also a big game for freshman Andrea Martin who had a double-double with 23 points and 11 rebounds despite being in foul trouble. “I thought I wasn’t going to get back in. When I went out, I just thought, ‘Don’t foul.’ Just to calm down and keep my composure. I just left it all on the court tonight,” freshman Andrea Martin said. Also making a strong impression was freshman Savannah Dennig with 18 points. She came off the bench for her strong game. “Knowing where the ball is and IQ on the court is something we really focused on. I don’t think coming off the bench isn’t that bad, it’s a game and we all get to play. We all know we have to put in enough whether you start or not,” Dennig said. Piedmont received the No. 9 seed in the Division 1 CIF State tournament, an impressive feat by a group with four freshmen, a sophomore, and just two juniors and seniors. They faced No. 8 Oakland Tech on Tuesday, March 4—results were not complete by Post time. “I’m really excited for what the season has for us. We just have to keep working, playing hard, executing, and working together,” Martin said. 70-48 blowout of No. 6 Salesian After a close 6-5 start to the game, Piedmont scored 11 and conceded just two to lead 17-7 before Salesian ended the quarter with a free throw. In the second quarter, Salesian inched closer at 22-18 with 4:25 left, but Piedmont rallied from there. PHS scored six straight and added a late free throw to go into halftime holding a 29-20 lead. In the third quarter, Salesian again made things close to trail 29-24 after a pair of baskets, Piedmont answered with 13 of the next 18 points to build a 42-29 lead. PHS ended the third with a 46-35 lead following two straight low post baskets by Dennig. Piedmont continued the outpour in the fourth with Saniyah Johnson hitting an early free throw, then finding Dennig for an assist – 49-35. articles.text: Staff Photos Ravi Silverberg has earned backto-back Athlete of the Month awards. With boys’ basketball, girls’ basketball, and boys’ soccer forging ahead in the North Coast Section playoffs and receiving berths in the CIF State playoffs, we’re awarding Ravi Silverberg of the boys basketball team and Gianluca Bini of boys soccer our boys’ Athlete of the Month, and Jenelle Solis and Andrea Martin of the girls’ basketball team as co-winners of Athlete of the Month. Ravi Silverberg has dominated for the boys’ basketball team. He’s now earned back-toback Athlete of the Month awards after being named our best boys athlete of January. In February, Silverberg carried the way after fellow scorer Dillon Casey suffered an injury at the very end of January. This NCS postseason, Silverberg scored 18 points in Piedmont’s 87-49 win over Ukiah in the first round on February 19, while he put up 25 points in their 78-69 quarterfinals finals win over Bethel on February 22— scoring his 1,000th career point in the process. In their semifinals’ 60-53 win over Windsor on February 26, Silverberg scored 17 points. Gianluca Bini earned one of our Athlete of the Week honors in February, proving vital to the boys’ soccer team’s NCS run in February. This postseason, Bini had one assist in Piedmont’s 2-0 win over Justin-Siena in the first round of the D4 playoffs on February 19. In the quarterfinals against No. 9 Urban on February 22, Bini logged two goals and on assist in their 2-0 win. He then scored another brace with two goals in their 2-nil win over San Rafael in the semifinals on February 26. Gianluca Bini earned an Athlete of the Month award for leading the soccer team through the NCS playoffs. Jenelle Solis was our honorable mention for Athlete of the Month in December and January, now earning the full award. She was recently named the Western Alameda County Conference’s Co-Player of the Year. In February’s NCS postseason, Solis logged 12 points and five assists in their 51-45 loss to No. 4 Cardinal Newman in the NCS Open Division first round on February 20. After that, Solis scored 10 and six assists in Piedmont’s 70-48 win over Salesian for fifth-place in the Open Division on February 26. articles.text: Sam Shelby wins two events Piedmont High’s track and field team competed in two events on Saturday, March 1, traveling to Westmont HS in San Jose for the K-Bell Track and Field Classic, and to Amador Valley in Pleasanton for the Dan Gabor Invitational. It was a strong start if the season for the Highlanders at the K-Bell with the boys’ team finishing second of 24 schools. The girls’ team was 15th of 25, while final team standings were not recorded at the Dan Gabor Invitational. At the K-Bell, Senior Sam Shelby had a monumental run in the 100 meter dash winning the event with a time of 11.05 seconds in a field of 133 runners. His time marked a personal record, shaving .05 off his previous mark. According to online records, Shelby is now just .81 behind Bill Hefter’s 100 meter school record of 10.24 set in 1961. Shelby is now No. 3 All-Time in the 400 meters, just .19 behind Bryan Chiang’s record set in 2008. Shelby also won the 400 meter run with a time of 50.74 against 66 other runners. His time was a four-second personal record, last running the event his sophomore year. “Sam’s a beast, simply put. He has a list of impressive goals for the season and as his coach, it’s easy to keep investing in him because he adjusts quickly and always delivers,” coach Pouyan Assadi said. Shelby was also a member of the 4x100 relay team as the second leg, alongside Reham Mumtaz, Maddox Ma, and Eric Venner. They placed second of 13 teams in 43.98. Also having an impressive day at the K-Bell was senior jumper Miguel Long. He won the long jump with a distance of 21 feet, 7.5 inches in a field of 44 athletes, while he was second of 29 in the triple jump in 41 feet, 11 inches. He was also 17th in the 400, 54.35. “Miguel has been claiming medals since he was a freshman, so another gold and silver comes to no surprise. He’s already hit the qualifiers for the Stanford Invitational, but he’s keen on hitting the Arcadia standard, which I think he can do if he has a nice couple weeks of practice,” Assadi said. Dash Waters-Worthen was also fourth of 19 in the 300 hurdles in 44.15. Aidan Ma was right behind him in fifth, clocking a 45.05. As for the girls, their 4x100 relay team of Nia Kim, Ella Yasar, Skye Prata-Baack, and Claire Aubrecht had a strong day by finishing second of 14 teams, clocking a time of 52.15. “Our girls 4x1 has two new members but we didn’t miss a beat. Graduating Breah Bell leaves some giant shoes to fill, but Ella and Claire are taking on leadership roles and Nia and Skye have stepped up,” Assadi said. Yasar also competed in two other events. She was 12th of 84 in the 100 with a time of 13.45, while she was ninth of 56 in the 400 in 1:04.30. At the Dan Gabor Invitational, Piedmont’s boys’ and girls competed in the 800 and 1600 meter runs. For the boys, Sebastien Swain was 25th of 263 in the 800 with a time of 2:05.80. Oliver Horsley also had a productive run in 50th, clocking a 2:09.30. As for the girls, sophomore Leighton Mand led the way in the 1600 with a time of 5:27.13, placing 19th of 218 runners. Skylar Best had a good run in 44th in 5:45.70, Caroline Taylor was 46th in 5:45.92, and freshman Nikita Gorelik was 49th in 5:46.72. In the girls’ 800, Gladwin Horsley was 58th of 159 in 2:41.10. NEXT UP Piedmont has three events this week. They compete in the Farmers Throw & Jumps Carnival on Friday, March 7 in Hayward, while they compete in the Bob Warren 55 at Acalanes in Lafeyette and the Ugly Eagles Relays at Clayton Valley Charter in Concord on Saturday, March 8. articles.text: In honor of the 75th anniversary of Children’s Fairyland, the Oakland Museum of California presents “Fairyland @ 75: A Legacy of Magic,” a vibrant retrospective exploring the history, evolution and cultural impact of America’s first storybook-themed amusement park. The exhibit, opening April 4 and on view through December 7, invites visitors to step into nearly eight decades of imagination, creativity and community at an Oakland institution that has shaped generations of childhoods. Museum visitors will discover a timeline of Fairyland’s history tracing the park’s journey from its inception and grand opening in 1950 to today; a “Then & Now” comparison of the attractions and their evolution over the decades; a photo collection of Magic Keys over the years highlighting the design evolution of this iconic Fairyland tradition; and a display of handcrafted miniatures created by local artists depicting scenes fromFairyland’s sets and attractions. Even more features to see at the exhibit include a display of memorabilia featuring rare artifacts, including an original Jolly Trolly car. Families can climb aboard one of Fairyland’s classic attractions and imagine the journey of Fairyland’s past to present. The exhibit opening on April 4 will take place during Friday Nights at OMCA, a vibrant weekly event from 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. where visitors can enjoy live music, sample delicious food, participate in hands-on activities and explore the museum’s exhibits into the night. “For 75 years, Fairyland has been a space where children and families escape the ordinary, immerse in imaginative play and bring stories to life,” said Kymberly Miller, CEO of Children’s Fairyland. “We’re thrilled to partner with another Oakland institution, OMCA, to celebrate Fairyland’s incredible journey and its enduring role in Oakland’s cultural landscape. “A joyful exemplar of Oakland’s vitality, Fairyland has provided delight and wonder to countless East Bay residents and visitors for the past 75 years and counting,” added Lori Fogarty, Oakland Museum CEO. “We are thrilled to host this new installation at OMCA and to partner with our neighbor and beloved cultural anchor.” The Oakland Museum of California (1000 Oak St.) is open 11 a.m. through 5 p.m., Wednesday through Sunday, with later hours for adults on Thursdays 5 p.m. to 8 p.m., and for all on Fridays 5 p.m. to 10 p.m. Tickets (adults $19; seniors $16; youth, students and educators $12; children 12 and under free) and more information are available at museumca.org. “Fairyland @ 75: A Legacy of Magic,” is a vibrant retrospective in celebration of the 75th anniversary of Children’s Fairyland, on view at the Oakland Museum of California April 4 through December 7. ®

articles.text: Impressionism fans, mark your calendars for this one: From Friday, March 21 through July 2026, San Francisco’s Legion of Honor will reunite Claude Monet’s extraordinary group of Venetian paintings. The exhibition will mark the first dedicated exploration of Monet’s luminous Venetian works since their debut in 1912, placing them in context with select paintings from key moments throughout his career, and in dialogue with portrayals of the city by artists such as Canaletto, Édouard Manet, John Singer Sargent, J. M. W. Turner and Pierre-Auguste Renoir. The exhibit will bring together more than 20 of Monet’s Venetian views from public and private collections around the world, including two masterpieces from the collections of the Brooklyn Museum and the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco — The Doge’s Palace and The Grand Canal, Venice. The fact that half of Monet’s Venice paintings are in private collections today makes this project a once-in-a-lifetime experience of the majestic city that inspired one of the most famous artists in the history of Western art. Claude Monet, The Grand Canal, Venice, 1908. From Friday, March 21 through July 2026, San Francisco’s Legion of Honor will reunite Claude Monet’s Venetian paintings for the first time since their debut in 1912. Monet himself once remarked that Venice was “too beautiful to be painted,” and it is perhaps this very beauty, and the city’s fame that has obscured the significance and daring nature of the works he produced there. Often overshadowed by his iconic depictions of the French landscape, Monet’s Venetian works are among the most luminous yet underexplored work of his career. Although Monet visited Venice only once, the city had a profound impact on him. With its fragile beauty and delicate interplay of land and sea, Venice became a site of both formal experimentation and symbolic resonance for the artist. Unlike the bustling, populated scenes of Venetian imagery painted by other artists such as Canaletto, Monet’s Venice is almost uncannily devoid of human presence. His focus was instead on rendering the city’s architecture and canals emerging through and dissolving in the encompassing and unifying color and light that he described as the envelppe. In addition to Monet’s paintings of Venice, the exhibition will present more than a dozen other works created throughout his career that show his lifelong fascination with water and reflections. Paintings from Monet’s time in Normandy, London, and his home at Giverny — including some of his famed water lily canvases — will be on view, drawing connections between the artist’s Venetian experiments and his broader oeuvre. Monet’s trip to Venice was his last major international journey. He returned invigorated, with a new perspective on the water lily paintings he was creating in Giverny. As Monet himself said, “My trip to Venice has had the advantage of making me see my canvases with a better eye.” “In 10 weeks in 1908 Monet captured Venice’s ethereal cityscape in shimmering canvases, creating works unlike anything produced by the centuries of artists who painted the city before him,” described Thomas P. Campbell, Director and CEO of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco. “Exploring Monet’s alongside other artists’ paintings of Venice deepens our understanding of his innovations in capturing the atmospheric effects of the Venetian lagoon on canvas.” The Legion of Honor (100 34th Ave.) is open 9:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., Tuesday through Sunday. Tickets ($20 adult, $17 senior, $11 student, free under 18) are available at ticketing.famsf.org, or at the front desk.

articles.text: classical and American jazz traditions at Old First Presbyterian Church in San Francisco this Sunday. Pianist Utsav Lal and saxophonist George Brooks will fuse Indian classical music and American jazz with contemporary minimalism, crafting innovative new sounds at a concert at Old First Presbyterian Church in San Francisco this Sunday, March 9 at 4 p.m. This extraordinary hybrid concert collaboration will create a genre-defying soundscape that bridges cultures and traditions. The performance will feature a mix of composed and improvised material, inspired by the rich structures of Indian music and American improvisation. Utsav Lal, the acclaimed “Raga Pianist” and Young Steinway Artist, is a visionary Indian pianist and composer who has redefined the role of the piano in Hindustani classical music. With a career spanning two decades, Lal’s soulful renditions of traditional songs have captivated audiences worldwide, with performances at leading venues such as Carnegie Hall, The Kennedy Center, Southbank Centre and NCPA. Blending ancient tradition with innovation, Lal’s unique piano style is influenced by South Indian vocal “Dhrupad” music and artists like The Necks and Thelonious Monk George Brook s is a n award-winning saxophonist and composer renowned for bridging jazz and Indian classical music. He founded influential Indian fusion groups including Summit with Zakir Hussain; Bombay Jazz with Ronu Majumdar and Larry Coryell; Raga Bop Trio with Steve Smith and Prasanna; Kirwani Quartet with Pt. Hariprasad Chaurasia; and Elements with Kala Ramnath and Gwyneth Wentink. Brooks began his jazz studies with Count Basie saxophonist Frank Foster and continued at the New England Conservatory with George Russell, Joe Allard, and Jaki Byard. His journey took him to India, where he studied Indian classical music with Pandit Pran Nath. His albums are considered groundbreaking in the fusion of jazz and Indian classical music. Tickets ($30 general, $25 senior, $10 students with ID, 12 and under free) are available at oldfirstconcerts.org.

articles.text: The magnificent Vienna Philharmonic returns to Berkeley with three programs of symphonic masterworks with maestro Yannick Nézet-Séguin at the podium, tonight through the Cal Performances 2025 Gala celebration on Friday, March 7. One of the most in-demand conductors in the world, NézetSéguin seems to be everywhere at once. Now at the helm of this orchestra. the Grammy-winner NézetSéguin also leads the Philadelphia Orchestra and the Metropolitan Opera Orchestra, and was musical advisor for the Leonard Bernstein biopic Maestro, for which he also recorded the soundtrack. The March 5 concert matches Mozart’s brilliant Jupiter Symphony with Mahler’s dramatic and ambitious Symphony No. 1. The March 6 performance pairs the sweet lyricism of Franz Schubert’s Symphony No. 4 with Antonín Dvořák’s well-loved New World Symphony, with the orchestra’s brass section featured in the latter work’s haunting slow movement. The final concert in the series on March 7 welcomes esteemed pianist Yefim Bronfman for Richard Strauss’ Ein Heldenleben, Op. 40, and Beethoven’s Piano Concerto No. 3, an intensely dramatic work. “Nézet-Séguin didn’t merely keep time or hold the Philharmonic together; he led them with passion and decisive interpretation …. His finales were so rousing, the audience began to cheer before Nézet-Séguin had even lowered his baton,” wrote the New York Times. Cal Performances Gala This year’s gala, centered around the Philharmonic’s closing night performance on March 7, will feature a cocktail reception at 5:30 p.m. under a grand tent in Lower Sproul Plaza and a 9 p.m. dinner on the stage of the nearby Zellerbach Playhouse. The 2025 Gala dinner is designed by Paul Canales, former chef and owner of the revered East Bay restaurants Duende and Occitania, and former executive chef of Oliveto. Canales, a longtime music fan, ls a friend of composer and MacArthur Fellowship winner John Zorn. International food author Marcella Hazan praised him, writing, “Paul Canales has found and taken unfailing command of what everyone who cooks struggles to discover: the straight road to pure, sincere, deeply satisfying flavor.” Wine for the 2025 Gala is provided by Hess Persson Estates. McCalls Catering & Events, Got Light, Stuart Event Rentals, and Soirée Valet have been engaged to design the event. Following the event Drew Altizer Photography will offer images of it. The honorary chairs and presenting sponsors of the 2025 Gala, Maria Manetti Shrem and Elizabeth Segerstrom, will both be honored with the California Performing Arts Visionary Award at this year’s event. Gordon P. Getty is the 2025 Gala’s Grand Benefactor. Tickets (concert $50-$225; gala $500-$100,000) for these events at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall are available online at calperformances.org, by email at tickets@calperformances.org or by phone at 642- 9988. articles.text: Brandee Younger plays new compositions with New Century Chamber Orchestra Tomorrow night through Sunday, March 9 at SFJAZZ, see harpist Brandee Younger present an exciting new set of compositions from her forthcoming album. For this four-night residency at the venue — 7:30 p.m. through Saturday and 7 p.m. on Sunday — Younger will be accompanied by a superb ensemble featuring acclaimed pianist Courtney Bryan and the 19-piece New Century Chamber Orchestra under the direction of bassist, composer and producer Derrick Hodge. SFJAZZ Executive Artistic Director and seven-time Grammy winner Terence Blanchard has said “Brandee Younger is a powerhouse of the harp. Those two words aren’t usually put together. In this case, it speaks to her creative genius and her passion for music.” Carrying on and expanding the tradition of pioneering jazz harpists Dorothy Ashby and Alice Coltrane, Younger made her public debut in 2007 as a grad student at New York University, when saxophonist Ravi Coltrane enlisted the then-23-year-old to participate in a memorial service for his mother Alice. A student of jazz great Jackie McLean, Younger has collaborated with artists from the worlds Tomorrow night through Sunday, March 9 at SFJAZZ, see harpist Brandee Younger present exciting new work with the pianist Courtney Bryan and the New Century Chamber Orchestra. of jazz and hip hop, including Jack DeJohnette, Charlie Haden, Pharoah Sanders, Lauren Hill and Common. In 2021 she released her Impulse! Records debut, Somewhere Different, which earned Younger a Best Instrumental Composition GRAMMY nomination for the track Beautiful is Black, making her the first Black woman nominated for this honor. In 2024, she was the winner of an NAACP Image Award. The New York Times has said of her: “Brandee Younger has almost single-handedly made a persuasive argument for the harp’s role in contemporary jazz.” Rolling Stone has said “Younger’s playing, virtuosic but with a sparkling lightness, invites you to set aside questions of classification, and just savor the sonic finery.” New Orleans native Courtney Bryan is a 2023 MacArthur Fellow and composer-in-residence with Opera Philadelphia. She has composed for orchestras and chamber groups all over the world and collaborated with artists including Kara Lynch, Sharan Strange and Branford Marsalis. Tickets ($25-95) and more details for the shows at SFJAZZ (201 Franklin St.) are available at sfjazz.org, or through the box office at 415-788-7353.

The performances mark Kentridge’s eagerly anticipated return to Berkeley following the success of his production SIBYL. This new work, conceived in collaboration with choral conductor and dancer Nhlanhla Mahlangu and theater maker Phala Ookeditse The Bay Area premiere of The Great Yes, The Great No, South African artist William Kentridge’s latest play will be performed Friday, March 14 through Sunday at Zellerbach Hall. Phala, is a chamber opera set on a 1941 sea voyage from Marseille to Martinique. The Great Yes, The Great No is rooted in the historic wartime escape from Nazi-occupied Vichy France by the surrealist André Breton, anthropologist Claude Lévi-Strauss and Cuban artist Wifredo Lam/ It fictionalizes this narrative by adding a colorful cast of historical characters to the passenger list that includes Josephine Baker, Leon Trotsky and Joseph Stalin. Kentridge assembles this menagerie of eccentric thinkers, makers and revolutionaries to make connections between surrealism and the anticolonial Négritude movement, a cultural, political and literary movement founded by a group of African and Caribbean students in Paris in the 1930s who sought to reclaim the value of African culture. Kentridge’s intention in the work is to explore dreamlike, surreal approaches to language and image inspired by both movements. Internationally acclaimed for his visual art, opera and theater productions, Kentridge deploys his signature visual language in the new production, combining animated drawings, video projection, masks, shadow play and bold sculptural costumes with spoken and projected text. Surrealist imagery merges with reallife events and South African choral music, dance and poetry. With its splicing together of recorded events and associative fiction to generate provocative new narratives, Kentridge’s treatment readily opens up to accommodate multiple layers of connection and inquiry about issues that remain urgently significant, including artistic and political critiques of the legacy of colonialism; experiences of political displacement; and what Kentridge terms “the spasms of history”: abrupt moments of personal transformation triggered by the unresolved political events. Rather than offer an “historical reenactment of an event,” The Great Yes, The Great No “becomes a commentary on the themes that were running through the world at that time, as well as contemporary reflections on the historical event,” said Jeremy Geffen, executive and artistic director of Cal Performances. “Though it will be recognizable as a William Kentridge artwork, the style is very different from that of his previous Sibyl,” Geffen added. Because it takes South African artist William Kentridge off from an actual historical event, The Great Yes, The Great No becomes “a much more narrative work, but the Surrealist elements of the piece take you out of the story that it tells in multiple ways … it ventures into absurdity. It’s sometimes difficult to distinguish between what is actual history and what is reflection. There is drama, but there is a lot of humor as well. All of it is so engaging.” Tickets ($43-$130) for this show at UC Berkeley’s Zellerbach Hall are available online at calperformances.org, by email at tickets@calperformances.org or by phone at 642- 9988.

articles.text: The Renegade Orchestra is returning to the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Saturday, March 8, at 7:00 p.m. Led by conductor Jason Eckl, the orchestra pairs award-winning string musicians with rock-and-roll in a show that encourages the audience to dance and let down their hair. The orchestra mixes top Bay Area string players with a hard-hitting rhythm section to create something that is, in their words, the opposite of elevator music. The strings are a mix of symphony playing, wedding string quartets, Grammy Award winning, Juilliard graduating violins, violas and cellos while the rhythm section consists of a range of players from North Beach jazz musicians to recent college grads. The musicians who take time out of their busy performing schedules to play in the Renegade Orchestra have been entertaining audiences since 2021 with string arrangements of “Purple Haze”, “Bohemian Rhapsody”, “Sweet Home Alabama”, “Enter Sandman” among others. The Bay Area-based rock orchestra came roaring out of lockdown with its first show selling out in Oakland. The group’s second show 24 hours later was at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, playing on the front lawn because of social-distancing rules at the time. “We did one out on the lawn and it went very well, though we couldn’t get the construction to stop initially,” said Eckl, recollecting the orchestra’s first visit to Piedmont. “After a lot of begging, we got everybody to stop jackhammering nearby and all that kind of stuff, and then we did this beautiful outdoor performance on the lawn. We actually haven’t played indoors there yet.” The Renegade Orchestra is coming to Piedmont after performing back-to-back sold out shows – especially impressive considering their difficulty finding a willing venue to play at. “If we call an orchestra venue, the minute they see rock and roll, they get scared. If we call a rock venue, the minute they see orchestra, they get scared. So the hardest part is finding a venue that isn’t afraid of either the orchestra portion or the rock-androll portion,” said Eckl. Tickets are available for $30 at https://bit.ly/RenegadeOrchestra_piedmont or renegadeorchestra.com. The Renegade Orchestra Photo by Frederic Aube

The legendary Glenn Miller was one of the most successful of all dance bandleaders starting with the Swing Era of the 1930’s and 40’s. A matchless string of hit records, the constant impact of radio broadcasts, and his drawing power at theatres, hotels and dance pavilions built and sustained his popularity. The first is a love story between two kindred spirits, Tami Oldham (Shailene Woodley) and Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin), both twenty-something. The year is 1983. The place Tahiti. Tami, who left her home in San Diego right out of high school, began to drift from port to port throughout the South Pacific, working odd jobs, crewing on boats and tourist ships. She is newly arrived in Tahiti when she meets New Zealander, Richard Sharp (Sam Clafin), having just arrived on his trim 36 foot schooner, the Mayaluga. Almost immediately they begin a relationship, nurtured by the gorgeous beaches, long sails on Richard’s boat, strolls through outdoor marketplaces, awash in color, easy-does-it people. All is kissed by soft trade winds gently blowing through. The two relish being together, their carefree lives, while sharing a world view that takes them out and about while embracing an existence far off the grid. Of course, Richard asks Tami to join him in his travels and they plan their sail from Tahiti to places east. But unexpectedly, Richard meets two fellow sailors from London who propose to hire him to sail their spectacular boat, with all the possible comforts available on a 45 footer, from Tahiti to San Diego, which is Tami’s hometown. The offer is sweetened with $10,000 and two first-class tickets back to Tahiti after the boat is delivered. The money, Tami and Richard conclude, could keep them sailing for at least a year, and so they decide to leave the Mayaluga in Tahiti and make the trip. And so begins act three, which is the most intense part of the film, but also something I will avoid mentioning in this review. I’ll say that this is a compellingly entertaining film, especially wellacted by Shailene Woodley who is most convincing, not only in her connection to Richard when they are in Tahiti, but her all-in performance in act three. Full disclosure: I love sailing movies. I love the idea of sails filled with wind and the absolute silence, other than the sound of halyards banging softly against the mast, or waves hitting the bow and sending up a welcoming spray that reaches the cockpit. I spent a lot of time doing all of the above on the San Francisco Bay, out by Alcatraz, and over by Tiburon, with Sausalito in the distance. But there is a caveat: blue water sailing is profoundly different and requires a sustained diligence that acknowledges the full measure of the sea and its power. Which Adrift graphically conveys. articles.text: Meryl Streep in River Wild River Wild is an engaging, fastpaced adventure-thriller set on a challenging Idaho white water river. The film opens with Gail Hartman (Meryl Streep) preparing to leave with her tween son Roarke (Joseph Mazello) and her husband, Tom Hartman (David Strathairn), packing for their trip west. Gail grew up on the river where she was once a guide, and will act as their principal rower. The getaway trip is clearly a much anticipated and needed family holiday; it’s also a birthday present for Roarke who has heard from his mom all about the roller coaster excitement that awaits him. Arriving, absent Tom, at least initially (he arrives last minute), the family, now including Tom, launches in a typical whitewater raft from a placid starting point. Gail, confident and eager to school her son on the skill sets necessary to navigate the river, takes the oars and so the trip begins. As they drift along, the river current grows stronger and the excitement slowly builds. On their second day, they spot a beached raft and two men on the shore and Gail rows toward the shore to say hello. And it’s at this point in the trip that a tone of tension begins to build. One of the men, Wade (Kevin Bacon), asks Gail if they can follow them on the river, explaining that he and friend are first-timers on the raver and insist they want to attempt a section of the river that is potentially dangerous. What was meant to be a mildly exciting summer holiday trip for the family soon grows in intensity. River Wild features strong performances by Streep and Bacon, as well as Strathairn. It’s a solid thriller. River Wild. Directed by Curtis Hanson. Starring Meryl Streep, Kevin Bacon, David Strathairn. 1 hr., 15 min. Rated PG-13. Streaming on Netflix/Fandango/Prime/ apple tv. Abrams was tasked with telling not only the final chapter of what has been a 42-year, nine-film saga, first brought to the screen in 1977, but he was also asked to neatly tie a knot in an array of plot and genealogical threads. And, of course, it was expected that he would catch lightening in a bottle. Of course. there’s the Star Wars fandom, the meta-audience that will reflexively scrutinize and deconstruct, via social media, every action scene and every brief moment of exposition while simultaneously being pleased and cranky. But taking a step back, it’s impossible not to acknowledge that the Star Wars franchise, in the aggregate, is a work of extraordinary imagination that has, from it first moments, resonated with generations of moviegoers and had a remarkable cultural impact. articles.text: William Shatner and Leonard Nimoy in Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home The year was 1966 and a Sci Fi series called Star Trek debuted on television, promising to “boldly go where no man has gone before.” Now, more than 50 years later, improbably, Star Trek remains a not forgotten cultural phenomenon. For a time it was not only a television syndication of the original show, but generated books, comics, video games and, for a time, a themed attraction in Las Vegas that drew thousands of what came to be known as “Trekkies.” In other words, Star Trek evolved from those early days in the 60s into a worldwide entertainment juggernaut, resonating with generations of fans, and possessing a cult following wherein hard-core Trekkies perused endless layers of narrative minutiae, characterization and predictive technology. In 1979 the first feature length film was made – Star Trek: The Motion Picture — launching what would become a successful franchise that starred the original multiethnic cast from the television series. Names such as Spock (Leonard Nimoy), Captain Kirk (William Shatner), Lt. Uhura (Nichelle Nichols), and “Bones” McCoy (DeForest Kelley) were a familiar part of our lexicon, as was the phrase, “beam me up.” In fact, NASA named its prototype space shuttle the Enterprise after the fictional starship. Of all the Star Trek films made, including a prequel, perhaps the most accessible is Star Trek IV: The Voyage Home, receiving four Oscar nominations. You don’t have to be a Trekkie to enjoy this movie. Though it follows Star Trek III: The Search for Spock, IV easily stands alone. PRESENTS

articles.text: Classic cars are certainly popular these days. When you go to a museum and see Ferrari and Bugatti cars, it sends shivers through your soul. What do you think of first? Is it the classic style? How about speed and agility? Maybe you’re looking for something that’s beautiful. What about the cost? What do you think of when you see a violin bow? You probably think: “a bow is a bow as a rose is a rose.” Let’s compare classic cars with classic violin bows. There are many similarities. Most people think that a violin bow is just a stick of wood with horse hair between the two ends. You turn a screw at one end to tighten and loosen the horse hair. That’s what most people think. But let me give you something to think about. A violin bow is one of the most astonishing inventions of mankind. It is so cunningly contrived that nothing else can do the work for which it is designed to do. It is a perfect tool. No mathematician, draftsman or craftsman could produce a better tool than the violin bow. It is at the same time unbelievably sensitive to touch. It is truly the work of genius. articles.text: It was one of those winter storms the TV news like to call an “atmospheric river” as my colleague Wayne Marzolf and I drove over the bridge towards Napa. We were headed to one of my favorite wine tastings of the year - the annual Zinfandel Advocates and Producers (ZAP) at the COPIA Center in Napa on February 1. This year the ZAP organizers had really stepped up their game and had invited some really fine restaurants and chefs to provide food designed to go with Zinfandel. Even with the poor weather the room was packed and full of great aromas and vibrant energy. Zinfandel is not native to California – most ampelographers from UC Davis now believe it came to California from Croatia in the 1800s, but it’s certainly the trademark grape of the state; there was even a bill before the state legislature to declare it the official state wine (the Cabernet and Pinot producers protested). Ninety nine percent of the world’s Zinfandel is grown in California and because there is no French equivalent it is the closest thing we have to a native son. World class Zinfandels are still much less expensive than world class California Cabernets but unfortunately the price is edging upward. Most of the wines listed below retail for between 25 and 50 dollars. These wines can often be found at lower prices at places like the Wine Club in SF or on Wine.com. The wonderful thing about Zinfandel is how versatile it is in pairing with food. It goes great with salmon, steak, burgers, pasta or pizza to say nothing of enjoying a glass all on its own. There were so many old standby producers as well as some new kids on the block that I was excited to meet. The overall quality was extremely high making my job of discerning the best wines very tough. At the end of the day the following wines were the ones that stood out. They are the cream of the crop. • 2021 Seawolf Zinfandel Only one barrel of this Mendocino County micro-Zinfandel was made. The side project for winemakers Jesse and Emma Hall has deep and inviting aromas of tar and earth mingling with red berry fruit and spices. It is fresh and clean with bracing acidity made in a food friendly style. This delicious Zin is worth searching out. • 2022 Miro Zinfandel Bastoni Vineyard Miro Tcholakov who also makes the Trentadue wines is a perennial resident in the top Zinfandel’s circle. This year his Bastoni Vineyard Zin was the standout. The nose is marked by scents of redcurrants and gentle herbal shadings, the palate is full-bodied but taut and juicy, with silky tannins and ample length. • 2023 Perlegos Zinfandel Stampede Vineyard This Lodi based vineyard has given us a wine with a nose of cranberries and blueberries, touches of earth, licorice and orange peel. The palate is medium bodied with dense berry fruits, pleasantly chewy tannins and good freshness on the finish. Excellent effort. • 2023 Once and Future Zinfandel Teldeschi Vineyard It was not surprising to see Zinfandel master Joel Peterson’s current project Once and Future in the top circle again. He is again producing wine from some of the iconic vineyards that made Ravenswood famous. articles.text: Mark your calendars. On the Waterfront, one of the most esteemed of American films, will be playing free to viewers next week at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. One of the rewarding pleasures of movies is seeing a film with friends and then chatting about it when the lights come up. That’s just what Piedmont’s Flix Fest, which meets on the second Thursday of each month, offers: a great movie in a comfortable setting, and then a lively discussion of it afterward. This month’s offering from 1954 was helmed by Elia Kazan, for whom it won a best director Academy Award. Its compelling story centers on a New Jersey dockworker, Terry Malloy (Marlon Brando), who was an up-and-coming boxer until a vicious local mob boss, Johnny Friendly (Lee J. Cobb), forced him to throw a fight. When a longshoreman is murdered to prevent him from testifying about Friendly’s control of the waterfront, Terry teams up with the dead man’s sister, Edie (Eva Marie Saint), and a streetwise priest, Father Barry (Karl Malden), to testify himself. The scene in which Terry’s older brother Charley (Rod Steiger), tries to dissuade him from speaking up is one the most famous in movie history. It’s the “I coulda been a contender” scene, containing, many have said, the finest example of acting in any American film. It’s heartbreaking. On the Waterfront won numerous awards, including best picture, best actor for Marlon Brando, and best supporting actress for Eva Marie Saint. Leonard Bernstein’s edgy musical score deserved an award, too. On the Waterfront will be screened on Thursday, March 13th, at 1:00 p.m. at the Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Doors will open at 12:45. The event is free and available to anyone over 18 years of age. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis, though registration is encouraged at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Everyone is welcome to bring snacks or lunch. The next movie in the Piedmont series is the charming French comedy Amelie, to be screened on April 10th.

articles.text: It was a warm, sunny, springlike morning last Wednesday for the Walking on Wednesdays group. A large turnout of 54 walkers and two K-9 best friends was on hand. February is recognized as Black History Month and it was an opportunity to consider Piedmont’s Black history. The group’s first destination was the Wildwood Avenue former home of the Sidney Dearing family, the first Black family to own a Piedmont house. The group could also later learn about Tom Williamson, who was the first African American student in Piedmont. The walkers went down Magnolia Avenue to 67 Wildwood Avenue and stopped in front of the house where a sad piece of Piedmont’s history was shared. Newspaper articles of the time said Dearing was a successful café owner “whose blood is Indian and white, but sufficient of the black to mark him negro.” Their house was purchased for $10,000 in January 1924 by Dearing’s mother-in-law, who was White. pages.text: Wednesday, March 5, 2025 27 Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers explore Piedmont’s racial history It was a warm, sunny, springlike morning last Wednesday for the Walking on Wednesdays group. A large turnout of 54 walkers and two K-9 best friends was on hand. February is recognized as Black History Month and it was an opportunity to consider Piedmont’s Black history. The group’s first destination was the Wildwood Avenue former home of the Sidney Dearing family, the first Black family to own a Piedmont house. The group could also later learn about Tom Williamson, who was the first African American student in Piedmont. The walkers went down Magnolia Avenue to 67 Wildwood Avenue and stopped in front of the house where a sad piece of Piedmont’s history was shared. Newspaper articles of the time said Dearing was a successful café owner “whose blood is Indian and white, but sufficient of the black to mark him negro.” Their house was purchased for $10,000 in January 1924 by Dearing’s mother-in-law, who was White. She transferred it to Dearing and his biracial wife. When this was learned, a Piedmont citizens committee offered to buy the home from Dearing for $3,000 more than was paid for it, and he and his family would have to leave the city. Dearing refused. The City said if he didn’t accept their offer, it would start condemnation and eminent domain proceedings so that a supposed extension of Fairview Avenue could be built through to Wildwood Avenue. During this contentious period, a brick was thrown through the window of the Dearing home and a bomb large enough to damage several blocks was found near the home. The Alameda County sheriff provided protection for the residents, but the Piedmont Chief of police, who as a member of the KKK, did not. In May of that year, a crowd of more than 500 people gathered in front of the home and refused to disperse until Dearing agreed to sell the house and leave Piedmont. Dearing finally agreed to accept $25,000, $15,000 of which was for “the surrender of his constitutional rights.” Dearing sold the house in February 1925 and he and his family moved to Oakland. The Piedmont City Council is developing a Sidney and Irene Dearing Memorial Project in Triangle Park at Magnolia and Wildwood Avenues, across the street Tom Willamson from where the Dearings lived on Wildwood. This project began in May 2022 when the City Council directed the Park Commission to develop recommendations for a memorial. A subcommittee talked with descendants of the Dearings and others to develop a set of guiding project principles. The City has engaged Oakland-based landscape architect Walter Hood to develop memorial designs. The walkers took a group photo in front of the former Dearing and then went to Palm Drive, Wallace Avenue, and past the Wildwood School playground where staff member Mike Carter was getting ready for the noon Tom Willamson high school track photo rush. The group stopped nearby and looked at Witter Field below. A better piece of Piedmont’s Black history was shared, that of Tom Williamson. Walker Nancy Olsen was a 1964 classmate and friend of Tom, and she shared her memories of him. Tom excelled both academically and athletically at Piedmont High, was student body president, and earned letters in football, basketball and track and field. He attended Harvard where he was an All-East defensive back on the football team. He graduated magna cum laude, and was a Rhodes Scholar at the same time as Bill Clinton. He earned his law degree at UC Berkeley in 1974, and had a distinguished legal career marked by public service. Tom died in 2017 at the age of 70 from pancreatic cancer. Meghan Bennett’s History of Piedmont website has an excellent page on Tom, https://www.historyofpiedmont.com/tom. It was then time to go back to the Exedra. The walkers found a steep extension of Requa Road on Wildwood, just past the steps down to Witter Field. The road provides access to four lovely, hidden Requa homes. The Requa extension might be a little like Black History in Piedmont. Many people don’t know about it. Some parts are hard, some parts are beautiful but exploring it can help us get to where we need to be. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. pages.text: 28 Wednesday, March 5, 2025 AMERICANS IN PARIS The Women of French Impressionism By Patricia Forsyth Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on March 16, 2022 The French are proud of the females who are recognized Impressionists. Art historian Henri Focillon, a professor at Académie Beaux Arts, wrote in 1928 that he deemed three women to be serious Impressionists, les trois grandes dames, Berthe Morisot, Mary Cassatt and Marie Bracquemond. The works of the three females were “revolutionary,” according to Artnet, bringing the feminine sensibility by portraying the real lives of ordinary people. One of the women, the American expat Mary Cassatt, lived most of her life in France and was extraordinarily successful both critically and commercially. Her themes of “mother and child” were universal and insightful forays into women’s inner life. Another of the trio, Marie Bracquemond was a gifted artist who lived “under the thumb” of her artist-husband Félix, the chief saboteur of her art legacy. Their son Pierre later wrote about his parents’ relationship, calling out Felix’s jealousy of his wife’s talent and the successes she enjoyed Balcony, Édouard Manet, 1868. Berthe (left) sat for the artist. Déjeuner sur l’herbe, by Édouard Manet, 1863, the artist’s provocative painting. Berthe at Easel, by Edma Morisot at Salon and the Louvre. They worked together at Havilland, creating porcelain dinnerware and pottery bowls. A 2018 retrospective of Marie’s work reintroduced her to the French public as a major artist. In comparison, the life and work of Berthe Morisot is well known to the French, but The Paris Review noted that Musée D’Orsay’s ushered Berthe Morisot into the collection many decades later than the male artists. The Morisot sisters Édouard Manet was already a cause celebré when Berthe Morisot and her sister Edma were introduced to him by a mutual friend, painter Henri Fantin-Latour who had intimated the sisters were noticeably promising painters. Édouard wrote to Fantin-Latour that, “they’re delightful sisters,” but “what a pity they can’t be men.” He was clearly annoyed by the waste of art training on women. To date, no women had been recognized as serious artists, and yet he was astounded by their confidence and ambition. Edma and Berthe enjoyed all the advantages that the Victorian era could possibly provide. They were intelligent and educated. Their father was an architect in government service and their mother was a distant relative of the rococo Jean-Honoré Fragonard and supported their daughters’ enthusiasm for art instruction. The parents built a studio at home and enlisted A-list artists, especially the Barbizon trailblazer Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot who praised the girls for their quick learning and skills. Berthe qualified for the annual Impressionist exhibition at age 23, and as she matured, she exhibited her work yearly for more than a decade. Her painting style was loose with fast brushwork radiating confidence, but she was shadowed by self-doubt.
